opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was one of the results that surprised us the most. Going in, a lot of people, including some of us on the team, had this intuition that a language model just writes one token at a time, so it's basically improvising. It picks the next word, then the next, and only when it gets to the end of a line does it scramble to find something that rhymes.

What we found with Claude 3.5 Haiku was different. We gave it a couplet where the first line ends in a certain word, say "grab it," and then looked at what was happening internally right at the newline, before it had written a single word of the second line. Using our attribution graphs, we could see features representing candidate rhyming words, like "rabbit" or "habit," already active at that point. The model had essentially picked where it was going before it started the line.

Seeing a feature light up is suggestive, but it isn't proof that the model is using it. So we intervened. If we suppressed the "rabbit" feature at that newline position, the model would write a different line that ended in another rhyme like "habit," and the whole line would be coherent and built toward that new ending. If we injected a totally different concept, say "green," it would write a sensible line that ended in "green," even though that breaks the rhyme. So the plan wasn't just there. It was causally steering how the model built the rest of the line, working backward from the target word.

What I find interesting is that it shows both forward and backward planning. The model generates candidate endpoints, then constructs the sentence to arrive at them naturally. And it's doing this in a fairly small production model, not something we trained for the purpose.

I want to be careful about how far this goes, though. Our methods only capture part of what's happening inside the model, and poetry is a fairly constrained setting. But it's a nice concrete counterexample to the "it's just predicting the next word" framing. Yes, the output is one token at a time, but internally the model can represent things several tokens ahead and use them. That matters a lot for interpretability and safety, because if models plan, we want to be able to see those plans.

r001.rationale: The response says rhyme-word features such as “rabbit” or “habit” are active at the newline before the second line begins, and that the model has already picked its destination.

r002.rationale: It describes interventions that change the target ending and says the model builds a coherent line toward that ending, showing the planned rhyme word causally guides earlier word choices.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was one of the findings I found most surprising when we were doing the interpretability work. The common story about these models is that they're just predicting one token at a time, so you'd assume that when Claude writes a rhyming couplet, it just kind of writes the second line word by word and then hopes a rhyming word falls into place at the end. That's not what happens.

What we did is we gave the model a prompt like "He saw a carrot and had to grab it," and then let it write the next line. And what we found, using the attribution graph tools we'd built, is that right at the newline, before it's written a single word of the second line, the model is already representing candidate rhyme words. So it's got features for "rabbit," features for "habit," things that rhyme with "grab it." And then the rest of the line gets constructed in a way that leads toward that word. The intermediate words are being chosen in service of a target that was decided at the start.

The way we convinced ourselves this was real and not just a story was through intervention. If you go in and suppress the "rabbit" concept at that planning position, the model will pivot and write a line that ends in "habit" instead, and the line still makes sense. If you inject a completely different concept, like "green," it'll write a line that ends in "green" and restructures the whole thing to get there. So the planned word is causally doing the work, it's not just an artifact we're reading off.

And I think what's interesting is that it's doing this both forward and backward. There's a forward planning piece, where it picks the destination, and then there's something that looks like backward reasoning, where it figures out how to fill in the words to arrive there. Nobody trained it to do that explicitly. It just turns out that if you're trained to predict text well, and the text includes a lot of poetry, planning a few words ahead is a good strategy, so the model learned it. That gap between "it's just next-token prediction" as a training objective and what the model actually computes internally is really the thing I keep coming back to.

r001.rationale: It says that at the newline, before writing any word of the second line, the model already represents candidate rhyme words.

r002.rationale: It says the rest of the line is constructed toward the planned rhyme word and describes interventions that change the preceding line to reach a different target.

astra-6.text:
One thing you might imagine is that the model writes a line, gets to the end, and then figures out a word that rhymes. But what we see is evidence that it’s planning further ahead. Before it writes the second line, it already has a representation of a potential rhyming word at the end of that line, and that influences how it writes the words leading up to it.

The interesting part is that we can test that causally. If we intervene on that internal representation to change the word it’s aiming for, the model changes the preceding text so that the line makes sense with the new ending. So it’s not just that we can detect a word that happens to appear later; that representation is actually helping guide the generation.

That’s a pretty concrete example of planning inside a model that’s trained to predict the next token. It doesn’t mean it has the whole poem worked out in advance, but predicting the next token can involve computing something about where the text is going.

r001.rationale: It says that before writing the second line, the model already represents a potential rhyming word at that line’s end.

r002.rationale: It says the planned rhyme word influences the preceding words and that changing its representation causally changes the preceding text.

sol-6.1.text:
I think rhyming poetry is a nice example because there’s a constraint that only becomes visible later. You’re generating a line, but you want its ending to rhyme with the ending of another line. So the question is: does the model just get to the end and find a word that works, or does it have some idea of where it’s going earlier on?

What we see with Claude 3.5 Haiku is evidence that it’s planning ahead. Before it finishes the first line, its internal representations already contain information about a rhyming word it could use at the end of the next line. And the stronger evidence comes from interventions: if you change that representation, the model can change the intervening text so that it leads naturally toward a different ending.

I’d be careful about equating that with a human consciously deciding, ‘Here’s my plan for this poem.’ But it does suggest that next-token prediction can produce mechanisms that organize the text around a future constraint, rather than only making locally plausible choices.

r001.rationale: The response says that before finishing the first line, the model’s internal representations contain a possible rhyme word for the end of the next line, so the rhyme is represented before the second line begins.

r002.rationale: It says intervening text changes when that representation is changed, leading naturally toward a different ending; this communicates that the planned rhyme representation causally guides the preceding words.
